children: Gold prices climbed more than 2.5% on Monday, recovering some ground after their steepest weekly decline since March as investors await fresh U.S. inflation data for more clues on the Federal Reserve's next move.
Futures in New York rose 2.9% to $3,616.80 a troy ounce. Despite the rebound, prices remain roughly 10% lower for the month following last week's sharp selloff.
"Precious metals are trading sharply higher, supported by a recovery in equities and oversold conditions," analysts at Saxo Bank said. "Last week's weakness was primarily a liquidity-driven event."

The decline was driven by heavy selling across equity markets amid concerns over the AI industry's build-out, expectations of higher interest rates and a stronger U.S. dollar, which makes dollar-denominated commodities like gold more expensive for overseas buyers.
"Gold prices falling initially during equity sell-offs is a common pattern," analysts at Goldman Sachs said. "Gold's liquidity makes it a source of cash during sharp risk-asset sell-offs."

The latest rebound comes as traders remain focused on the Fed's monetary-policy outlook. Markets are pricing in a 96% probability of a 25-basis-point interest-rate increase in December, according to CME FedWatch data, while expectations for a larger, half-percentage-point move have been priced out.

That outlook, however, could shift again Wednesday, when the U.S. personal-consumption expenditures price index--the Fed's preferred inflation gauge--is released. A stronger-than-expected reading could reinforce expectations of further monetary tightening, potentially putting renewed pressure on non-yielding gold.
Other precious metals also advanced on Monday. Silver futures rose 2.6% to $42.16 an ounce, while platinum gained 1.3% to $1,306.80 an ounce.

Still, a rapid rebound is not guaranteed. Some hedge funds could remain reluctant to rebuild positions ahead of year-end, while the prospect of a December rate increase provides another reason for investors to delay adding to gold holdings, Goldman analysts said.
